content: Currently, there is no definitive evidence to determine the optimal feeding interval for very preterm infants. Shorter feeding intervals, such as every two hours, theoretically allow for smaller milk volumes per feed, which may reduce the incidence and severity of gastroesophageal reflux. Conversely, longer feeding intervals, such as every three hours, may allow for more complete gastric emptying between feeds, potentially providing rest periods for the immature digestive system and reducing hyperemia. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety of shorter feeding intervals (two hours or less) compared to longer feeding intervals (three hours or more) in very preterm infants. The outcomes assessed included the time required to regain birth weight, the time to achieve full enteral feeding, and secondary outcomes such as hospital stay duration, episodes of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and growth parameters (weight, length, and head circumference) during hospitalization. A systematic search was conducted using Cochrane Neonatal's standard methodology, including databases such as CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and CINAHL, as of June 25, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs comparing short (e.g., one or two hours) versus long (e.g., three or four hours) feeding intervals in preterm infants born at less than 32 weeks' gestation were included. Eligible studies involved nasogastric or orogastric bolus feeding with either breast milk or formula, where the feeding interval was the primary intervention. Four RCTs involving 417 infants were included in the review, with one additional study involving 350 infants awaiting classification. All included studies compared two-hourly versus three-hourly feeding intervals. The risk of bias was generally low, although all studies had a high risk of performance bias due to the inability to blind the intervention. Three studies (351 participants) were included in a meta-analysis for the time taken to achieve full enteral feeding. The mean time to achieve full feeds ranged from eight to 11 days. The analysis found little to no difference between two-hourly and three-hourly feeding intervals in terms of days to achieve full enteral feeding, but the certainty of this evidence was low (mean difference [MD] ‒0.62 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] ‒1.60 to 0.36). Low-certainty evidence suggested that infants receiving two-hourly feeds may take slightly longer to regain their birth weight compared to those receiving three-hourly feeds (MD 1.15 days, 95% CI 0.11 to 2.20; 3 studies, 350 participants). The effect of shorter feeding intervals on secondary outcomes, such as hospital stay duration (MD ‒3.36 days, 95% CI ‒9.18 to 2.46; 2 studies, 207 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and the risk of NEC (typical risk ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.11; 4 studies, 417 participants; low-certainty evidence), remains uncertain. None of the included studies reported on growth parameters during hospitalization. In conclusion, the available low-certainty evidence suggests that there may be no clinically significant differences between two-hourly and three-hourly feeding intervals in very preterm infants. However, there is insufficient data regarding potential feeding complications, particularly NEC. Additionally, no studies have evaluated other feeding intervals, and there is a lack of long-term data on neurodevelopmental outcomes or growth. Further research is needed to address these gaps.
